summary: This April 1st joke RFC specifies Scenic Routing for IPv6, a humorous scheme in the spirit of Green IT in which packets are routed to get as much fresh-air time as possible. It is not meant to be implemented.

plainLanguage.summary: This April 1st joke proposes routing IPv6 packets through wireless links or avian carriers to give them more fresh-air time. It describes an option for expressing those preferences.

questions: what is scenic routing in rfc 7511
subtitle: An April 1st IPv6 joke proposes choosing routes for packets' fresh-air time.

tldr.problem: This April 1st joke says packets should get fresh air rather than travel through underground fiber paths.
tldr.mechanism: It proposes an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Scenic Routing Option that signals whether scenic routes, avian carriers or wireless links may be used or preferred.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational joke document; the RFC says there are no IANA actions at this time.

today: RFC 7511 is an Informational April 1st joke document. It is not presented as an adopted routing standard.

sections.title: The Scenic Routing Idea
sections.content:
RFC 7511 is an April 1st joke about Green IT. Instead of focusing on reducing energy use, it proposes routing IPv6 packets to get as much fresh-air time and sunlight as possible.

The RFC suggests that a routing engine might choose paths using Avian IP Carriers or wireless technologies. It focuses on IPv6 and says it ignores communication based on Vintage IP.
sections.plainLanguage: This April 1st RFC jokes that packets should get outside. Its proposed route choices favor wireless links and avian carriers.

sections.title: The Scenic Routing Option
sections.content:
The Scenic Routing Option is placed in an IPv6 Hop-by-Hop Options Header. The RFC proposes option identifier 0x0A and an 8-bit option length greater than zero. The option parameter encodes urgency, whether Avian IP Carrier and wireless links may be used, and an affinity for one link type.

Every node en route must preserve the option if it is present. The RFC says the two lowest bits are reserved for future use and that multiple SROs must not appear in one datagram.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed option records how strongly a packet prefers scenic routing. It can also allow or prefer avian-carrier and wireless links.

sections.title: Routing Implications
sections.content:
If scenic routing is requested, the path with the known longest avian-carrier or wireless portion must be used. The RFC suggests that backbone operators could prepare separate MPLS paths for this purpose.

Hosts and relaying applications are also told how to carry the option into packets they send. The RFC discusses security considerations for avian and wireless links and notes that user route choices could affect traffic engineering.
sections.plainLanguage: The proposed rule makes the route with the most wireless or avian-carrier travel take priority. It also notes possible effects on network traffic engineering.
